questions.q: A farmer fences a rectangular vegetable plot 90 m long and 65 m wide with 2 rounds of wire. Ignoring the gate and the knots, the wire needed is:
Tanvi has a 56 cm length of wire. She bends it, without any overlap, into a rectangle whose length is 19 cm. The breadth of her rectangle is:
questions.a: 9 cm

questions.q: A school track has a perimeter of 180 m. Gurpreet runs 1,000 m along it, starting from the starting line. Which statement describes where she is?
questions.a: She has finished 5 full rounds and is 100 m along her sixth round.
o: She has finished 5 full rounds and is 100 m along her sixth round.
She has finished 5 full rounds and is 80 m along her sixth round.
She has finished 6 full rounds and is back at the starting line.
She has finished 5 full rounds and is 10 m along her sixth round.

questions.q: A rectangular mirror frame is 12 cm long and 5 cm wide. A shop makes a new frame with the length doubled and the width unchanged. The border length of the new frame is:
questions.a: 58 cm

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A rectangle 9 cm by 5 cm and a rectangle 8 cm by 6 cm need the same length of border.
Statement 2: Swapping the length and the breadth of a rectangle changes its perimeter.
Statement 3: A triangle with sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm has perimeter 18 cm.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: 2 x (length + breadth) does not change when the two numbers are swapped. Statement 1 is true (28 cm each) and statement 3 is true (5 + 5 + 8 = 18).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A rectangle with perimeter 18 cm and breadth 3 cm has a length of 15 cm.
Reason (R): The perimeter of a rectangle is 2 x (length + breadth).
questions.a: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true. The reason is true, but it gives length + breadth = 9 cm, so the length is 9 - 3 = 6 cm; the figure 15 comes from forgetting to halve the perimeter.
o: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.

questions.q: Tara walks 4 rounds along the edge of a square park of side 85 m. She covers a distance of ___ m.
A rectangle has perimeter 36 cm. Which of these must be true for it?
questions.a: Its length and breadth add up to 18 cm.
o: Its length and breadth add up to 18 cm.
Its length is 12 cm and its breadth is 6 cm.
Its length is twice its breadth.
Its sides are all 9 cm long.

questions.q: A triangular flag has sides 45 cm, 60 cm and 75 cm and gold lace is stitched along all three sides. (a) Find the length of lace needed. (b) The lace is sold only in whole metres at Rs 18 per metre. Find the amount paid.
questions.a: (a) 45 + 60 + 75 = 180 cm. (b) 180 cm = 1.8 m, so 2 whole metres are bought: 2 x 18 = Rs 36.
s: Part (b): rounds up to 2 m and gets Rs 36

questions.q: A notice board is 120 cm long and 80 cm wide. (a) Find the length of border strip needed to go around it once. (b) The same strip is bent into a square frame. Find its side, and say whether it lies between 80 cm and 120 cm.
questions.a: (a) 2 x (120 + 80) = 400 cm. (b) Side = 400 / 4 = 100 cm, which lies between the breadth 80 cm and the length 120 cm.
s: Part (b): side 100 cm and it lies between 80 and 120

questions.q: True or False: If the length of a rectangle is increased by 3 cm and its breadth is decreased by 3 cm, its perimeter stays the same.
questions.a: True. The new perimeter is 2 x ((length + 3) + (breadth - 3)) = 2 x (length + breadth), which is the old perimeter.
s: Reason: length + breadth is unchanged, so 2 x (length + breadth) is unchanged

questions.q: A student finds the perimeter of a 10 cm by 4 cm rectangle as 4 x 10 = 40 cm. (a) Find the correct perimeter. (b) Say when the student's method would give the right answer.
questions.a: (a) 2 x (10 + 4) = 28 cm. (b) The method 4 x length is right only when the breadth equals the length, that is, when the rectangle is a square.
s: Part (b): right only for a square

questions.q: Along the boundary of a shape drawn on a square grid, there are 7 straight segments of one grid-side each and 3 diagonal segments, each across one small square. (a) Write the perimeter in the form _s + _d. (b) Anil says the perimeter is exactly 10 units. Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 7s + 3d. (b) No. A diagonal of a small square is longer than its side, so the 3 diagonals together are more than 3 units and the perimeter is more than 10 units.
s: Part (b): diagonal is longer than a side, so more than 10 units

questions.q: Kabir says, 'A square of side 15 cm and a rectangle 20 cm by 10 cm need the same length of ribbon, because 15 + 15 = 30 and 20 + 10 = 30.' Test his claim.
questions.a: Kabir is right. The square needs 4 x 15 = 60 cm and the rectangle needs 2 x (20 + 10) = 60 cm. His working compares length + breadth (half the perimeter) for each, and equal halves give equal perimeters.
s: Perimeter of the square is 60 cm
Perimeter of the rectangle is 60 cm
Explains that equal sums of two adjacent sides give equal perimeters

questions.q: Show that no rectangle with whole-number sides in centimetres can have a perimeter of 25 cm.
questions.a: The perimeter is 2 x (length + breadth). If length and breadth are whole numbers, length + breadth is a whole number, so twice it is an even number. 25 is odd, so it cannot be the perimeter.
s: States that twice a whole number is even

questions.q: Write a real situation that the expression 3 x 2 x (50 + 30) describes, and say what each number stands for. Then evaluate it.
questions.a: A watchman walks 3 rounds around a rectangular godown 50 m long and 30 m wide. (50 + 30) is length + breadth, 2 x (50 + 30) = 160 m is one round, and 3 x 160 = 480 m is the distance walked.
s: A situation with a 50 m by 30 m rectangle and 3 rounds
Identifies 2 x (50 + 30) as one round and 3 as the rounds

questions.q: A school ground is 110 m long and 70 m wide. It is fenced all around except for an 8 m gate gap, and the fencing costs Rs 45 per metre. Find the cost.
questions.a: Perimeter = 2 x (110 + 70) = 360 m. Fenced length = 360 - 8 = 352 m. Cost = 352 x 45 = Rs 15,840.
s: Subtracts the gate gap to get 352 m

questions.q: Karan runs 4 rounds on an outer rectangular track 80 m by 50 m. Divya runs 6 rounds on an inner rectangular track 70 m by 40 m. (a) Find the distance each runs. (b) Who runs farther, and by how much? (c) What is the least whole number of rounds Karan must run on his track to cover at least as much as Divya?
questions.a: (a) Outer track: 2 x (80 + 50) = 260 m, so Karan runs 4 x 260 = 1,040 m. Inner track: 2 x (70 + 40) = 220 m, so Divya runs 6 x 220 = 1,320 m. (b) Divya runs farther, by 1,320 - 1,040 = 280 m. (c) 1,320 / 260 is a little over 5, so Karan needs 6 rounds (1,560 m).
s: Part (a): both perimeters, 260 m and 220 m
Part (a): the distances 1,040 m and 1,320 m

questions.q: Zoya has 120 cm of wire and bends it, without waste, into different shapes. (a) Find the side of the square she can make. (b) Find the breadth of a rectangle she can make with a length of 40 cm. (c) Two sides of a triangle she makes are 35 cm and 45 cm; find the third. (d) Say why all three shapes have the same perimeter although they look different.
questions.a: (a) 120 / 4 = 30 cm. (b) Length + breadth = 60 cm, so breadth = 20 cm. (c) 120 - 35 - 45 = 40 cm. (d) Each shape uses the whole wire once around its boundary, and perimeter is only the total length around the boundary, whatever the shape.
s: Part (d): same wire gives the same total boundary length

questions.q:
A school in Nashik plans a rectangular vegetable garden 24 m long and 18 m wide, fenced all around except for a 3 m gap kept for the gate. Quote A: wire at Rs 35 per metre plus Rs 450 labour, with no gate. Quote B: Rs 3,300 fixed price including a new gate. The school already has an old gate that can be reused.
(a) Find the perimeter of the garden. (b) Find the length of wire needed. (c) Find the total cost under Quote A. (d) Decide which quote the school should take and give one reason using your figures.
questions.a: (a) 2 x (24 + 18) = 84 m. (b) 84 - 3 = 81 m. (c) 81 x 35 + 450 = Rs 3,285. (d) Quote A costs Rs 15 less, and the old gate can be reused, so A is the cheaper sensible choice; B would suit the school only if the old gate is unusable, because then it buys the gate for a price near A's.
s: Part (d): a decision using Rs 3,285 against Rs 3,300 and the old gate

questions.q:
A coach marks the edge of a rectangular practice field 75 m long and 45 m wide with a cone every 5 m, starting at one corner. Students must run 2,000 m. The coach can let them run only whole rounds, or whole rounds plus a stretch along the edge.
(a) Find the perimeter of the field. (b) Find the number of cones. (c) After 8 full rounds, how far is a student from 2,000 m, and where on the edge does she finish if she runs the rest? (d) The coach must choose between 8 full rounds and 9 full rounds. Which is closer to 2,000 m, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 2 x (75 + 45) = 240 m. (b) 240 / 5 = 48 cones, because 75 and 45 are both multiples of 5. (c) 8 rounds = 1,920 m, so 80 m remain; she crosses the 75 m side and finishes 5 m along the 45 m side. (d) 8 rounds is 80 m short; 9 rounds is 2,160 m, 160 m over. So 8 rounds is closer, by 80 m against 160 m.
s: Part (c): 80 m left and 5 m past the first corner
Part (d): chooses 8 rounds with 80 m against 160 m

questions.q: A craftsman glues gold lace along the edge of a hexagonal photo frame with six equal sides and six equal angles. Each side is 18 cm. The lace needed is:
questions.a: 108 cm

questions.q: Mansi bends a 72 cm wire into a regular hexagon. She then straightens it and bends it into an equilateral triangle. The side of the triangle is:
questions.a: 24 cm

questions.q: A paper rectangle 8 cm by 6 cm is cut along the middle into two equal 8 cm by 3 cm pieces. The pieces are joined end to end along their 3 cm edges to make one long strip. Its perimeter compared with the original rectangle's 28 cm is:
questions.a: 38 cm, which is 10 cm more

questions.q: A shop cuts triangular flags with all sides equal and a whole-number side in centimetres. Which perimeter can such a flag NOT have?
questions.a: 64 cm

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A regular hexagon of side 6 cm has perimeter 30 cm.
Statement 2: A square is a regular polygon, so 4 x side is the same rule as number of sides x side.
Statement 3: Cutting a rectangle into two pieces and rejoining them differently keeps the area but can change the perimeter.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: 6 x 6 = 36 cm, not 30 cm. Statements 2 and 3 are true.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two 8 cm by 3 cm pieces joined end to end along their 3 cm edges have a larger perimeter than the same two pieces joined along their 8 cm edges.
Reason (R): Joining along a shorter edge hides less boundary than joining along a longer edge.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion. Joining along 8 cm hides 2 x 8 = 16 cm of the 44 cm in total (perimeter 28 cm); joining along 3 cm hides only 2 x 3 = 6 cm (perimeter 38 cm).
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Each regular shape below has a perimeter of 60 cm. Match the shape in Column I with its side in Column II.
Column I: 1. regular pentagon  2. regular hexagon  3. equilateral triangle  4. square
Column II: a. 20 cm  b. 15 cm  c. 12 cm  d. 10 cm
Two regular polygons have the same side length of 10 cm. The perimeter of one is 20 cm more than the perimeter of the other. How many more sides does it have?
questions.a: 2 more sides

questions.q: A rangoli border is a regular pentagon with each side 15 cm. (a) Find the length of the border. (b) If the artist changes it to a regular hexagon with the same side, by how much does the border length increase, and why does it equal that amount?
questions.a: (a) 5 x 15 = 75 cm. (b) 6 x 15 = 90 cm, an increase of 15 cm, because the hexagon has one more side and each side is 15 cm.
s: Part (b): increase of 15 cm explained by one extra side

questions.q: A 90 cm wire is made into an equilateral triangle and then, in another try, into a regular hexagon. (a) Find the side in each case. (b) Explain why the hexagon's side is half the triangle's side.
questions.a: (a) Triangle: 90 / 3 = 30 cm; hexagon: 90 / 6 = 15 cm. (b) The same wire is shared among twice as many equal sides (6 instead of 3), so each side is half as long.
s: Part (b): twice the sides, so half the length each

questions.q: True or False: When a rectangle is cut into two pieces and the pieces are rejoined without overlap, the area of the new figure can differ from the area of the rectangle.
questions.a: False. No material is added or removed, so the total area stays the same; only the perimeter can change.
s: Correction: the area stays the same, the perimeter may change

questions.q: An 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle is cut into two equal 8 cm by 3 cm pieces. (a) Find the sum of the perimeters of the two pieces. (b) The pieces are joined end to end along their 3 cm edges and the perimeter becomes 38 cm. Use (a) to find how much boundary was hidden, and relate it to the 3 cm edge.
questions.a: (a) Each piece has perimeter 2 x (8 + 3) = 22 cm, so the sum is 44 cm. (b) 44 - 38 = 6 cm is hidden, which is 2 x 3 cm: the 3 cm edge of each piece is lost from the boundary.

questions.q: (a) State the property of a regular polygon that lets its perimeter be found by multiplying. (b) Use it to find the side of a regular 10-sided polygon whose perimeter is 85 cm.
questions.a: (a) All its sides are equal, so perimeter = number of sides x side. (b) 85 / 10 = 8.5 cm.

questions.q: Rohan says, 'If I cut a shape into pieces and rejoin them into a new shape, the area and the perimeter both stay the same, because nothing is added or taken away.' Test his claim with the 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle cut into two 8 cm by 3 cm pieces.
questions.a: Partly right. The area stays 48 sq cm because the same material is used. The perimeter does not have to stay: the original is 28 cm, but the pieces joined end to end along 3 cm edges give a 16 cm by 3 cm strip with perimeter 38 cm.
s: Agrees the area stays 48 sq cm
Shows the perimeter changes from 28 cm to 38 cm
Concludes: area unchanged, perimeter may change

questions.q: Show that a regular hexagon with a whole-number side in centimetres cannot have a perimeter of 100 cm, and name the two nearest perimeters it can have.
questions.a: Perimeter = 6 x side. 100 / 6 is about 16.67, not a whole number, so no whole side works. With sides 16 cm and 17 cm the perimeters are 96 cm and 102 cm.
s: Writes perimeter = 6 x side and divides 100 by 6
Notes 16.67 is not a whole number

questions.q: Write a real-life situation for the expression 6 x 25 cm that uses a regular polygon, and say what the answer measures.
questions.a: A florist edges a regular hexagonal flower tray with ribbon; each of the 6 equal sides is 25 cm. The answer, 150 cm, is the ribbon length, which is the perimeter of the tray.
s: A regular hexagon with 6 equal sides of 25 cm
Says 6 is the number of sides and 25 cm is one side

questions.q: A square of side 12 cm and an equilateral triangle of side 12 cm are joined along one full side to make a house-shaped figure. Find its perimeter and explain why it is not the sum of the two perimeters.
questions.a: The boundary has 3 sides of the square and 2 sides of the triangle: 5 x 12 = 60 cm. The two perimeters add to 48 + 36 = 84 cm, but the shared side is inside the figure, so 2 x 12 = 24 cm is hidden: 84 - 24 = 60 cm.
s: Explains the shared side is hidden, 84 - 24 = 60

questions.q: An 8 cm by 6 cm card is cut into two equal 8 cm by 3 cm pieces. (a) Find the perimeter of the original card. (b) Find the perimeter of one piece. (c) The pieces are joined end to end along their 3 cm edges; find the perimeter. (d) The pieces are joined along 8 cm edges but one is slid sideways so that only 4 cm of the edges touch; find the perimeter. (e) State what is the same in all arrangements.
questions.a: (a) 2 x (8 + 6) = 28 cm. (b) 2 x (8 + 3) = 22 cm. (c) 44 - 2 x 3 = 38 cm. (d) 44 - 2 x 4 = 36 cm. (e) The area, 48 sq cm, is the same in every arrangement.
s: Part (d): 36 cm using the 4 cm touching

questions.q: A decorator has 360 cm of ribbon and wants frames that are regular polygons with side 24 cm. (a) How many regular hexagon frames can she border, and how much ribbon is left? (b) The same for regular pentagon frames. (c) The same for equilateral triangle frames. (d) Which shape wastes no ribbon, and which gives the most frames?
questions.a: (a) Hexagon: 6 x 24 = 144 cm each; 2 frames, 72 cm left. (b) Pentagon: 120 cm each; 3 frames, 0 left. (c) Triangle: 72 cm each; 5 frames, 0 left. (d) Pentagon and triangle waste nothing; the triangle gives the most frames, 5.
s: Part (d): names pentagon and triangle as zero waste
Part (d): triangle gives the most frames

questions.q:
A craft shop has one reel of 400 cm of gold tape and makes coasters whose whole edge is bordered by the tape. Design H is a regular hexagon of side 6 cm, design S is a square of side 10 cm and design T is an equilateral triangle of side 15 cm. An order needs at least 10 coasters of one design, and the shop wants the least tape left over.
(a) Find the tape one coaster of each design needs. (b) How many coasters of each design can be made from the reel? (c) How much tape is left over for each design? (d) Which design should the shop use for this order? Justify with your figures.
questions.a: (a) H: 6 x 6 = 36 cm; S: 4 x 10 = 40 cm; T: 3 x 15 = 45 cm. (b) H: 11; S: 10; T: 8. (c) Left over: H 4 cm; S 0 cm; T 40 cm. (d) T makes only 8, so it fails the order. S makes exactly 10 with no tape left, matching the rule on waste. H makes 11 with 4 cm left, which is a spare coaster but not the least waste. The shop should choose S for this order, and H only if an extra coaster is worth more than 4 cm of tape.
s: Part (c): 4 cm, 0 cm and 40 cm left
Part (d): a decision checked against at least 10 coasters and least waste

questions.q:
A craft club cuts a 12 cm by 8 cm card into two equal 12 cm by 4 cm pieces and edges the new shape with tape costing Rs 2 per cm. Arrangement A joins the pieces along the 12 cm edges. Arrangement B joins them end to end along the 4 cm edges. In arrangement C the pieces touch along 7 cm of their 12 cm edges, one slid sideways. The club has Rs 100 and wants the finished shape to be at least 16 cm wide.
(a) Find the perimeter of one piece. (b) Find the perimeter of arrangements A, B and C. (c) Find the tape cost of each. (d) Which arrangement should the club use, given the budget and width? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 2 x (12 + 4) = 32 cm. (b) A: 2 x 32 - 2 x 12 = 40 cm; B: 64 - 2 x 4 = 56 cm; C: 64 - 2 x 7 = 50 cm. (c) A Rs 80; B Rs 112; C Rs 100. (d) B costs more than Rs 100. A is only 12 cm wide, below 16 cm. C is 12 + 5 = 17 cm wide and costs exactly Rs 100, so C meets both limits.
s: Part (d): chooses C, rejecting B on cost and A on width

questions.q: A rectangular hall is 8 m long and 6 m wide. It is to be covered with square tiles of side 40 cm. The number of tiles needed is:
A rectangular plot is 20 m long and 15 m wide. Two square flower beds of side 6 m each and one rectangular pond 8 m by 5 m are made inside it, with no overlap. The area left is:
questions.a: 188 sq m

questions.q: A farmer says his rectangular field has an area of 72 sq m and each side is a whole number of metres. Which pair of length and width could NOT be his field?
questions.a: 18 m and 5 m

questions.q: An L-shaped floor is made of a rectangle 10 m long and 4 m wide with a second rectangle 6 m long and 3 m wide joined below it along 6 m of its 10 m edge. The total floor area is:
questions.a: 58 sq m

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A rectangle 12 m by 3 m and a square of side 6 m have equal areas.
Statement 2: Every rectangle with perimeter 24 m has an area of 36 sq m.
Statement 3: Splitting an L-shaped figure into rectangles in two different ways gives two different total areas.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Statement 2 is false: a 10 m by 2 m rectangle also has perimeter 24 m but area 20 sq m. Statement 3 is false: the area of the figure is the same whichever way it is split. Statement 1 is true (36 sq m each).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Doubling the side of a square makes its area four times as large.
Reason (R): The area of a square is 4 times its side.
questions.a: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false. The reason is false: 4 x side is the perimeter. The area is side x side, so a side of 2s gives 2s x 2s = 4 s x s, which is four times the area.
o: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A rectangular plot 25 m long has an area of 450 sq m. Its width is ___ m.
A 9 m by 6 m rectangular lawn has a 3 m by 2 m rectangular bed cut out of it. Which expression gives the grass area in sq m?
A hall is 14 m long and 9 m wide and a square carpet of side 6 m is laid on it. (a) Find the floor area not covered by the carpet. (b) The uncovered part is polished at Rs 20 per sq m. Find the cost.
A verandah 9 m long and 6 m wide is covered with square tiles of side 3 m. (a) Find the area of the verandah and of one tile. (b) Find the number of tiles and the cost if one tile costs Rs 480.
questions.a: (a) Verandah 9 x 6 = 54 sq m; tile 3 x 3 = 9 sq m. (b) 54 / 9 = 6 tiles; 6 x 480 = Rs 2,880.
s: Part (a): 54 sq m and 9 sq m

questions.q: True or False: A square of side 7 m has an area of 28 sq m, because the area of a square is 4 times its side.
questions.a: False. 4 x 7 = 28 m is the perimeter. The area is 7 x 7 = 49 sq m.
s: Correction: 28 m is the perimeter; the area is 49 sq m

questions.q: A rectangular lawn 18 m long and 12 m wide has a rectangular pond 6 m by 4 m wholly inside it. (a) Find the grass area. (b) Seed costs Rs 15 per sq m of grass. Find the seed cost and say why the pond's position inside the lawn does not change it.
questions.a: (a) 18 x 12 - 6 x 4 = 216 - 24 = 192 sq m. (b) 192 x 15 = Rs 2,880. The grass area is the lawn area minus the pond area wherever the pond sits, as long as it is wholly inside.
s: Part (b): Rs 2,880 with the reason about position

questions.q: A student says the wire needed to fence a 30 m by 20 m field is 30 x 20 = 600 m. (a) What has she actually found, with its unit? (b) Find the wire needed for one round.
questions.a: (a) She found the area, 600 sq m, not a length. (b) The fence goes around the boundary: 2 x (30 + 20) = 100 m.

questions.q: Meena says, 'A square of side 12 m is exactly twice as large as a square of side 6 m, since the side is doubled.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Meena is wrong. The area of the 6 m square is 36 sq m and of the 12 m square is 144 sq m, which is 4 times as large, not twice. Doubling the side doubles the perimeter, not the area.
s: Areas 36 sq m and 144 sq m
Explains that the side doubles but the area is side x side

questions.q: Show that no square with a whole-number side in metres has an area of 50 sq m, and name the two nearest whole-number squares' areas.
questions.a: 7 x 7 = 49 and 8 x 8 = 64. A whole-number side of 7 m or less gives at most 49 and 8 m or more gives at least 64, so 50 sq m is not possible. The nearest areas are 49 sq m and 64 sq m.
s: Argues no whole side lies between 7 and 8
Names 49 sq m and 64 sq m

questions.q: Write a floor-and-carpet situation that the expression 20 x 15 - 4 x (3 x 3) describes, say what each part stands for, and evaluate it.
questions.a: A courtyard 20 m by 15 m has four square tulsi platforms of side 3 m. 20 x 15 = 300 sq m is the courtyard, 3 x 3 = 9 sq m is one platform, 4 x 9 = 36 sq m is all the platforms, and 300 - 36 = 264 sq m is the free ground.
s: A rectangle 20 by 15 and four squares of side 3
Identifies the parts of the expression

questions.q: A garden is 18 m long and 14 m wide. Three rectangular beds, each 4 m by 2 m, are made in it and the rest is lawn. Lawn seed costs Rs 12 per sq m. Find the cost of seeding the lawn.
questions.a: Garden area = 18 x 14 = 252 sq m. Beds = 3 x (4 x 2) = 24 sq m. Lawn = 252 - 24 = 228 sq m. Cost = 228 x 12 = Rs 2,736.
s: Garden area 252 sq m and beds 24 sq m

questions.q: A rectangular plot is 30 ft long and 20 ft wide. A line parallel to its 20 ft side divides it into a left part 12 ft wide and a right part 18 ft wide. The left part is two rooms: the top room is 12 ft by 8 ft and the bottom room fills the rest of the left part. The right part is one hall. (a) Find the area of the plot. (b) Find the dimensions and area of the bottom room. (c) Find the dimensions and area of the hall. (d) Check that the three areas add up to the plot.
questions.a: (a) 30 x 20 = 600 sq ft. (b) Its length is 20 - 8 = 12 ft, so it is 12 ft by 12 ft with area 144 sq ft; the top room is 96 sq ft. (c) The hall is 18 ft by 20 ft, area 360 sq ft. (d) 96 + 144 + 360 = 600 sq ft, equal to the plot.
s: Part (b): 12 ft by 12 ft, 144 sq ft
Part (c): 18 ft by 20 ft, 360 sq ft
Part (d): the sum 600 sq ft checks

questions.q: A farmer's rectangular field is 200 m long and 150 m wide. He sells a strip along the full 200 m length, 30 m wide. (a) Find the area of the field. (b) Find the area of the strip sold. (c) Find the area that remains. (d) Ploughing costs Rs 6 per hundred sq m; find the cost for the remaining land. (e) Say whether the remaining land is still a rectangle, with its dimensions.
questions.a: (a) 200 x 150 = 30,000 sq m. (b) 200 x 30 = 6,000 sq m. (c) 30,000 - 6,000 = 24,000 sq m. (d) 24,000 / 100 = 240 hundreds, 240 x 6 = Rs 1,440. (e) Yes, 200 m by 120 m, since the strip runs the full length; 200 x 120 = 24,000 checks.

questions.q:
A school hall is 24 m long and 15 m wide, with a stage of 8 m by 5 m built on part of the floor. The rest is to be tiled. Supplier X sells tiles only in packs that each cover 50 sq m, at Rs 4,500 per pack. Supplier Y sells by the square metre at Rs 95 per sq m, with no waste.
(a) Find the area of the hall. (b) Find the area to be tiled. (c) Find the cost with each supplier. (d) Which supplier should the school pick? Give one point in favour of the one you reject.
questions.a: (a) 24 x 15 = 360 sq m. (b) 360 - 8 x 5 = 320 sq m. (c) X: 320 / 50 is more than 6, so 7 packs = Rs 31,500; Y: 320 x 95 = Rs 30,400. (d) Y is Rs 1,100 cheaper. X leaves 350 - 320 = 30 sq m of spare tiles that could be used for repairs, which is a point in X's favour, so Y is the better pick unless spares are worth more than Rs 1,100.
s: Part (d): Y with Rs 1,100 saved and the spare-tile point for X

questions.q:
An orchard is 100 m long and 70 m wide. Each mango tree needs a square of ground 6 m by 6 m. The squares must not overlap and are laid in rows and columns parallel to the sides of the orchard. The farmer divides the orchard area by the area of one tree's square and plans to buy that many saplings.
(a) Find the orchard area. (b) Find the number of saplings the farmer plans to buy. (c) Find how many trees fit along the length and along the width, and in all. (d) Which number should he buy, and why do the two numbers differ?
questions.a: (a) 100 x 70 = 7,000 sq m. (b) 7,000 / 36 is about 194.4, so 194 saplings. (c) 100 / 6 gives 16 along the length and 70 / 6 gives 11 along the width, so 16 x 11 = 176. (d) He should buy 176. Whole squares cannot be cut: 4 m and 4 m are left over on the sides, so 7,000 - 176 x 36 = 664 sq m is unused, and area alone gives only an upper limit.
s: Part (d): 176 with the reason of unused strips (664 sq m)

questions.q: A leaf is traced on squared paper where each small square is 1 sq unit. It covers 14 squares fully, 6 squares more than half, 4 squares exactly half and 5 squares less than half. Using the counting convention, the estimated area is:
questions.a: 22 sq units

questions.q: A pond is traced on a grid in which every small square stands for a 2 m by 2 m patch of ground. It covers 9 squares fully, 5 squares more than half, 2 squares exactly half and 7 squares less than half. The estimated area of the pond is:
questions.a: 60 sq m

questions.q: Leaf A covers 12 squares fully, 3 more than half, 4 exactly half and 10 less than half. Leaf B covers 9 squares fully, 8 more than half, 3 exactly half and 2 less than half. Which leaf has the larger estimated area?
questions.a: Leaf B, by 1.5 sq units
o: Leaf A, because it touches more squares (29 against 22)
Leaf A, because it has more full squares (12 against 9)

questions.q: Four squares of a grid are covered by a shape to the extent of 100%, 60%, 50% and 45% respectively. Their contribution to the estimated area is:
questions.a: 2.5 sq units

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A grid square covered exactly half counts as half a square unit.
Statement 2: A square covered 51% counts as 1 unit and one covered 49% counts as 0, so a slight shift in tracing can change the estimate.
Statement 3: The estimated area of a shape on a grid is always exactly equal to its true area.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: the convention gives an estimate, which can be a little more or a little less than the true area. Statements 1 and 2 describe the rule correctly.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A shape that covers 6 squares fully and 4 squares exactly half has an estimated area of 8 sq units.
Reason (R): Squares covered less than half are ignored in the estimate.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion. The reason is a true part of the rule, but it plays no part in this count: 6 + 4 x 1/2 = 8 uses only full and exactly-half squares.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
A shape on a grid has six squares of one kind, or eight if full. Match each group in Column I with its contribution in Column II.
Column I: 1. 8 squares fully covered  2. 6 squares covered a little more than half  3. 6 squares covered exactly half  4. 6 squares covered a little less than half
Column II: a. 0 sq units  b. 3 sq units  c. 6 sq units  d. 8 sq units
Which set of squares gives an estimated area of exactly 7 sq units?
questions.a: 6 squares fully covered and 2 exactly half
o: 6 squares fully covered and 2 exactly half
6 squares fully covered and 2 more than half
5 squares fully covered and 3 exactly half
6 squares fully covered and 2 less than half

questions.q: A pond tracing shows 18 squares fully covered, 7 more than half, 5 exactly half and 9 less than half, each square being 1 sq m. (a) Find the estimated area. (b) A student counts every less-than-half square as 1/2 as well; find her estimate and say why it is probably too high.
questions.a: (a) 18 + 7 + 5 x 1/2 = 27.5 sq m. (b) 27.5 + 9 x 1/2 = 32 sq m. Each of those squares is covered by less than half, so giving it half a unit adds more than the shape really has.
s: Part (b): 32 sq m with the reason

questions.q: True or False: Two shapes that look very different can have the same estimated area on a grid.
questions.a: True. The estimate depends only on the counts of the four kinds of squares. For example, 12 full squares and 8 full plus 4 more-than-half squares both give 12 sq units, though the outlines differ.
s: Reason: the estimate is a total of counts, and different shapes can give the same total

questions.q: On a plan, each small square stands for a 2 m by 2 m plot. A patch of waste land covers 11 squares fully, 4 more than half and 3 exactly half. (a) Find its estimated area in sq m. (b) Levelling costs Rs 30 per sq m; find the cost.

Two students trace the same leaf on the same grid and get 24 and 26 sq units. (a) Give one reason both can follow the rule and still differ. (b) Which kind of square decides the difference in the rule?
questions.a: (a) A square covered close to half can look slightly more than half in one tracing and slightly less in the other, so it counts as 1 in one and 0 in the other. (b) The squares covered about half: the ones on the boundary of the more-than-half and less-than-half cases.
s: Part (a): near-half squares fall on different sides of half
Part (b): names squares covered about half

questions.q: A leaf covers 9 squares fully and 7 partly: 3 are more than half, 2 exactly half and 2 less than half. (a) Find the estimate by the rule. (b) A student counts all 7 partly covered squares as full. By how much does her estimate exceed the rule's?
questions.a: (a) 9 + 3 + 2 x 1/2 = 13 sq units. (b) She gets 9 + 7 = 16, which is 3 sq units more.

questions.q: Sana says, 'Squares less than half covered are ignored, so a grid estimate is always smaller than the true area.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Ignoring squares less than half covered loses a little area, but counting a more-than-half square as a whole gains area (a square 90% covered adds 10% too much). The gains and losses can go either way, so the estimate can be below or above the true area; it is not always smaller.
s: Accepts that ignored squares lose area
Shows counted more-than-half squares add extra
Concludes the estimate can be above or below

questions.q: A tracing has an estimated area of 12.5 sq units. Show that the number of exactly-half squares in it must be odd.
questions.a: Full squares and more-than-half squares add whole numbers, and less-than-half squares add 0. Only exactly-half squares add 1/2 each. For a total ending in .5 the number of halves must be odd, since an even number of halves adds a whole number.
s: Says only half squares add fractions
Says an even number of halves gives a whole number
Concludes the count must be odd

questions.q: Make up counts of full, more-than-half, exactly-half and less-than-half squares for a leaf whose estimated area is 20.5 sq units, and show the working.
questions.a: Sample: 15 full, 4 more than half, 3 exactly half and 6 less than half. Estimate = 15 + 4 + 3 x 1/2 + 0 = 20.5 sq units.
s: Counts that use all four kinds of squares
Adds the full, more-than-half and half contributions
Shows total 20.5 and ignores the less-than-half squares

questions.q: A pond is traced on a grid where each small square is a 3 m by 3 m plot. It covers 14 squares fully, 5 more than half, 4 exactly half and 6 less than half. Weeds are removed at Rs 7 per sq m. Find the estimated cost.
questions.a: Squares counted = 14 + 5 + 4 x 1/2 = 21. Area = 21 x 9 = 189 sq m. Cost = 189 x 7 = Rs 1,323.
s: Area 189 sq m using 9 sq m per square

questions.q: Using a grid where each small square is 2 m by 2 m, Pond P covers 16 squares fully, 5 more than half, 4 exactly half and 9 less than half. Pond Q covers 12 fully, 10 more than half, 2 exactly half and 3 less than half. (a) Find the estimated area of P in sq m. (b) Find that of Q. (c) Compare them. (d) Count the squares each pond touches and explain why the comparison of touched squares would mislead.
questions.a: (a) P: 16 + 5 + 2 = 23 squares, 23 x 4 = 92 sq m. (b) Q: 12 + 10 + 1 = 23 squares, 92 sq m. (c) The estimates are equal. (d) P touches 34 squares and Q touches 27, but the rule counts only the covered portion, so the shape touching more squares need not have more area.
s: Part (d): explains touching is not the same as covering

questions.q: A tracing has 10 fully covered squares and 12 partly covered squares. (a) What is the least the estimate can be? (b) What is the greatest? (c) If the 12 partly covered squares are 5 more than half, 4 exactly half and 3 less than half, find the estimate. (d) The tracer redraws the outline and every exactly-half square becomes just under half. Find the new estimate and the change.
questions.a: (a) If all 12 are less than half, the estimate is 10 sq units. (b) If all 12 are more than half, it is 22 sq units. (c) 10 + 5 + 4 x 1/2 = 17 sq units. (d) The 4 squares now count 0, so the estimate is 10 + 5 = 15 sq units, a fall of 2 sq units.

questions.q:
A forest officer traces a clearing on a grid in which each small square stands for a 5 m by 5 m patch. It covers 26 squares fully, 12 more than half, 8 exactly half and 15 less than half. A contractor plants saplings at Rs 80 per sq m, and the sanctioned budget is Rs 80,000.
(a) How many squares are counted? (b) Find the estimated area in sq m. (c) Find the cost for the whole estimated area. (d) The officer can ask for more money or plant on only part of the clearing. Which would you advise, and why, given that the area is only an estimate?
questions.a: (a) 26 + 12 + 8 x 1/2 = 42 squares. (b) 42 x 25 = 1,050 sq m. (c) 1,050 x 80 = Rs 84,000, which is Rs 4,000 above the budget. (d) Rs 80,000 pays for 1,000 sq m, 50 sq m short. Since the area is only an estimate that may be a little above or below the truth, asking for Rs 4,000 more (about 5% extra) secures the whole clearing; planting less is better only if the money cannot be raised.
s: Part (d): a justified choice that mentions the estimate and 1,000 sq m

questions.q:
After a flood, a muddy patch on a school courtyard is traced on a grid of 1 m squares. Priya counts 38 squares fully covered, 14 more than half, 6 exactly half and 17 less than half. A cleaning contractor charges Rs 22 per sq m. Later, Rohit traces the same patch and gets an estimate of 52 sq m.
(a) Find Priya's estimated area. (b) Find the cleaning cost on her estimate. (c) Find how much cheaper Rohit's estimate makes the job. (d) The principal must give the contractor one figure. Which estimate should she use, and what is the risk of the other?
questions.a: (a) 38 + 14 + 6 x 1/2 = 55 sq m. (b) 55 x 22 = Rs 1,210. (c) 52 x 22 = Rs 1,144, which is Rs 66 less. (d) Using 55 sq m makes sure enough money is set aside, with the risk of overpaying up to Rs 66 if 52 is nearer the truth. Using 52 sq m risks a shortfall of Rs 66 and a disagreement with the contractor if the patch is nearer 55. Either is defensible if the reason is stated.
s: Part (d): chooses one and states the risk of the other

questions.q: A tailor has a rectangular piece of cloth 24 cm long and 15 cm wide. He cuts it along one diagonal to make two triangular pennants. The area of one pennant is:
questions.a: 180 sq cm

questions.q: A triangular park has one side of 40 m along a road. Its opposite corner is 30 m from the road, measured at right angles to the road. Grass costs Rs 8 per sq m. The cost of grassing the park is:

In a rectangle 20 cm long and 8 cm wide, three triangles each use the whole 20 cm side as base. The first has its third corner at an end of the opposite side, the second at the midpoint of the opposite side and the third at a point 3 cm from one end of the opposite side. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: All three triangles have the same area, 80 sq cm.
o: All three triangles have the same area, 80 sq cm.
The second is the largest, because it is symmetrical.
The first is the smallest, because it has a right angle.
The third is the smallest, because its corner is off-centre.

questions.q: A triangular signboard has an area of 54 sq cm and a base of 9 cm. Its height is:
questions.a: 12 cm

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A rectangle cut along its diagonal gives two triangles, and the one on the longer side has the larger area.
Statement 2: A triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm has an area of 60 sq cm.
Statement 3: Two triangles can look very different and still have the same area.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Statement 1 is false: both triangles are exact copies of each other, so they have the same area. Statement 2 is false: the area is half of 10 x 6, which is 30 sq cm. Statement 3 is true.

questions.q:
In rectangle ABCD, E is a point on side DC and F is the point on AB directly below E.
Assertion (A): Triangle ABE has an area equal to half the area of rectangle ABCD, wherever E lies on DC.
Reason (R): Triangle AEF is half of rectangle AFED and triangle BEF is half of rectangle BFEC, and the two rectangles together make ABCD.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion. Adding the two halves gives half of (AFED + BFEC), which is half of ABCD whatever the position of E.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A triangle has an area of 84 sq cm and a base of 12 cm. Its height, in cm, is ___.
In rectangle ABCD, AB = 12 cm and AD = 8 cm. E is on side DC with DE = 5 cm, and F is on AB directly below E. The area of triangle AEF is:
questions.a: 20 sq cm

questions.q: A triangular flag has base 30 cm and height 24 cm and is cut from a rectangular cloth 30 cm by 24 cm. (a) Find the area of the flag. (b) What fraction of the cloth is wasted?
questions.a: (a) 1/2 x 30 x 24 = 360 sq cm. (b) The cloth is 720 sq cm, so 360 sq cm, which is 1/2 of it, is wasted.

questions.q: True or False: Keep the base AB of a triangle fixed on the lower side of a rectangle and move the third corner along the opposite side; the area of the triangle changes as the corner moves.
questions.a: False. The base and the height (the distance between the two sides) do not change, so the area stays half of the rectangle.
s: Correction: area stays half the rectangle since base and height stay the same

questions.q: A triangular plot has base 36 m and height 25 m. (a) Find its area. (b) A farmer sows 5 kg of seed per hundred sq m. How much seed does he need?

Rectangle ABCD is 14 cm long and 6 cm wide. E is on DC with DE = 4 cm and F is on AB directly below E. (a) Find the areas of triangles AEF and BEF. (b) Add them and show the result is half the rectangle.
questions.a: (a) AF = 4 cm and FB = 10 cm. AEF = 1/2 x 4 x 6 = 12 sq cm and BEF = 1/2 x 10 x 6 = 30 sq cm. (b) 12 + 30 = 42 sq cm, and half of 14 x 6 = 84 is 42 sq cm.
s: Part (a): 12 sq cm and 30 sq cm

questions.q: In a 16 cm by 10 cm rectangle, a blue triangle is formed by a diagonal and a red triangle has its third corner on the opposite 16 cm side, 5 cm from a corner. (a) Find the area of each. (b) Explain why the two look different but have equal areas.
questions.a: (a) Each is 1/2 x 16 x 10 = 80 sq cm. (b) Both have the same base, 16 cm, and the same height, 10 cm, so each is half of the same rectangle.
s: Part (b): same base and height, so both are half the rectangle

questions.q: Gopal says, 'In a rectangle ABCD, a triangle on base AB whose third corner is very close to D is thin and pointed, so its area is less than that of the triangle whose third corner is at the midpoint of DC.' Test his claim for AB = 12 cm and AD = 5 cm.
questions.a: Gopal is wrong. Both triangles have base AB = 12 cm and height 5 cm, so each has area 1/2 x 12 x 5 = 30 sq cm. A triangle looking thin does not change the base or the height, which fix the area.
s: Sets base 12 and height 5 for both triangles
Explains looks do not change base and height

questions.q: Show that a triangle drawn with its base along the 12 cm side of a 12 cm by 5 cm rectangle, and its third corner on the opposite side, cannot have an area of 40 sq cm.
questions.a: Any such triangle has base 12 cm and height 5 cm, so its area is 1/2 x 12 x 5 = 30 sq cm wherever the corner is. 40 sq cm is more than the 30 sq cm possible, so it is impossible.
s: Computes 30 sq cm for every position
Concludes 40 is more than 30, so impossible

questions.q: Write a real-life situation for the number sentence 1/2 x 24 x 15 = 180, saying what the 24, the 15 and the 180 mean.
questions.a: A sailmaker cuts a triangular sail with a base of 24 dm along the mast and a height of 15 dm from the base to the opposite corner. The area of the sail is 1/2 x 24 x 15 = 180 sq dm, half of the 360 sq dm rectangle that encloses it.
s: A triangle with base 24 and height 15
Names the 24 and 15 as base and height
Says 180 is the area, half of 24 x 15

questions.q: The front of a shed is a rectangle 10 m wide and 6 m high with a triangular gable above it of base 10 m and height 4 m. Painting costs Rs 55 per sq m. Find the cost of painting the front.
questions.a: Rectangle = 10 x 6 = 60 sq m. Gable = 1/2 x 10 x 4 = 20 sq m. Total 80 sq m. Cost = 80 x 55 = Rs 4,400.

questions.q: ABCD is a rectangle with AB = 16 cm and AD = 10 cm. E is on DC with DE = 6 cm, and F is the point on AB directly below E. (a) Find the area of ABCD. (b) Find the area of triangle BAD. (c) Find the areas of triangles AEF and BEF. (d) Find the area of triangle ABE and compare with (b). (e) Explain why the comparison comes out as it does.
questions.a: (a) 16 x 10 = 160 sq cm. (b) 1/2 x 160 = 80 sq cm. (c) AF = 6 cm and FB = 10 cm, so AEF = 1/2 x 6 x 10 = 30 sq cm and BEF = 1/2 x 10 x 10 = 50 sq cm. (d) ABE = 30 + 50 = 80 sq cm, equal to BAD. (e) Both have base AB and height AD, so each is half of the rectangle.
s: Part (d): 80 sq cm, equal to BAD

questions.q: A rectangular field ABCD has AB = 50 m and AD = 36 m. A point E on DC is 20 m from D and the farmer joins E to A and to B. (a) Find the area of the field. (b) Find the area of triangle ABE. (c) Find the areas of triangles ADE and EBC. (d) Check that the three areas add up to the field, and say where E must be to make ADE and EBC equal.
questions.a: (a) 50 x 36 = 1,800 sq m. (b) 1/2 x 50 x 36 = 900 sq m. (c) ADE = 1/2 x 20 x 36 = 360 sq m; EC = 30 m, so EBC = 1/2 x 30 x 36 = 540 sq m. (d) 360 + 900 + 540 = 1,800 sq m. They are equal when DE = EC = 25 m, the midpoint of DC.
s: Part (d): E at the midpoint, 25 m

questions.q:
A boat club has a rectangular canvas sheet 6 m long and 4 m wide that costs Rs 450 per sq m. Each sail is a triangle with base 6 m on the long edge and its third corner on the opposite long edge. A sail must have an area of at least 10 sq m. Cut A uses a diagonal and makes two sails from the sheet. Cut B puts the corner at the midpoint of the opposite edge, so the sail is symmetrical, and leaves two small triangles of 3 m by 4 m.
(a) Find the area and cost of the sheet. (b) Find the area of one sail. (c) Find the cost per sail for each cut. (d) The club wants a symmetrical sail. Is Cut B worth it? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 4 = 24 sq m; 24 x 450 = Rs 10,800. (b) 1/2 x 6 x 4 = 12 sq m for either cut. (c) Cut A yields two sails, so Rs 5,400 each. Cut B leaves two triangles of 1/2 x 3 x 4 = 6 sq m, each below the 10 sq m needed, so only one sail: Rs 10,800. (d) B costs Rs 5,400 more per sail for the symmetry. It is worth it only if the club values the symmetrical shape more than that; if cost matters most, Cut A is cheaper for the same 12 sq m of sail.
s: Part (c): Rs 5,400 and Rs 10,800 per sail
Part (d): a decision weighing Rs 5,400 more against symmetry

questions.q:
A farmer's rectangular field ABCD has AB = 60 m and AD = 40 m. A path from a point E on side DC to the corners A and B cuts it into three triangular fields ADE, AEB and EBC, with DE = 24 m. He has three sons and wants each to get an equal share.
(a) Find the areas of the three fields. (b) Check that they add up to the whole field. (c) Where would E have to be for ADE and EBC to be equal? (d) Can the three fields be made equal by moving E? Advise the farmer on a fair division.
questions.a: (a) ADE = 1/2 x 24 x 40 = 480 sq m; EC = 36 m so EBC = 1/2 x 36 x 40 = 720 sq m; AEB = 1/2 x 60 x 40 = 1,200 sq m. (b) 480 + 1,200 + 720 = 2,400 sq m = 60 x 40. (c) At the midpoint, DE = EC = 30 m, giving 600 sq m each. (d) No: AEB is always half of the field, 1,200 sq m, whereas an equal share would be 800 sq m. A fair plan with this layout is half to one son and 600 sq m to each of the other two; equal thirds need a different cut.
s: Part (c): E at the midpoint, 600 sq m each
Part (d): AEB is always 1,200 against 800, so equal thirds are impossible; offers a fair alternative

questions.q: A club wants a rectangular practice mat of 48 sq m with whole-number sides in metres and wants to spend the least on the rope that runs around its edge. Which dimensions should it choose?
questions.a: 8 m by 6 m

questions.q: Twelve square tiles of side 1 unit are joined edge to edge, with no gaps, to form a rectangle. The least possible perimeter, in units, is:
A figure made of unit squares has perimeter 24 units. A new unit square is attached so that two of its sides fit fully against the figure, in a notch. The new perimeter is:
questions.a: 24 units

questions.q: Shape A has an area of 18 sq units and Shape B has an area of 20 sq units. Shape A has the longer perimeter. Which pair of rectangles (length by breadth) could be A and B?
questions.a: A is 2 by 9 and B is 5 by 4
o: A is 2 by 9 and B is 5 by 4
A is 3 by 6 and B is 4 by 5
A is 3 by 6 and B is 2 by 10
A is 3 by 6 and B is 1 by 20

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Nine unit squares joined as a 3 by 3 block have a perimeter of 12 units, while the same nine in one row have a perimeter of 20 units.
Statement 2: A 4 by 6 rectangle and a 3 by 8 rectangle have equal areas but different perimeters.
Statement 3: A unit square attached to a figure along exactly one full side increases the perimeter by 2 units.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. Statement 1: 12 and 20 are correct. Statement 2: both have area 24, with perimeters 20 and 22. Statement 3: the new square adds 4 sides but hides 2 (its own side and the figure's side), a net rise of 2.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Among rectangles of area 24 sq units with whole-number sides, the 4 by 6 rectangle has the greatest perimeter.
Reason (R): The 1 by 24 rectangle has a perimeter of 50 units.
questions.a: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true. The reason is true, and it shows the assertion is false: 50 units is more than the 20 units of the 4 by 6 rectangle, which has the least perimeter.
o: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false.

questions.q:
Each rectangle below has an area of 30 sq units. Match the dimensions in Column I with the perimeter in Column II.
Column I: 1. 1 by 30  2. 2 by 15  3. 3 by 10  4. 5 by 6
Column II: a. 34 units  b. 22 units  c. 62 units  d. 26 units
An 18 m by 14 m rectangular plot is split by a line parallel to its 14 m sides into two plots, the first being 10 m long. The area of the second plot is:
questions.a: 112 sq m

questions.q: Sixteen unit squares are joined edge to edge into a rectangle with no gaps. (a) List the perimeters for all the rectangles that can be made. (b) State what stays the same and what changes across them.
questions.a: (a) 1 by 16 gives 34 units, 2 by 8 gives 20 units and 4 by 4 gives 16 units. (b) The area, 16 sq units, stays the same; the perimeter changes.

questions.q: True or False: Two rectangles can have the same perimeter and different areas.
questions.a: True. A 6 by 4 rectangle and a 7 by 3 rectangle both have perimeter 20 units, but their areas are 24 and 21 sq units.
s: Reason: example with perimeter 20 and areas 24 and 21

questions.q: Plot A is 20 m by 15 m and Plot B is 25 m by 12 m. (a) Find the area and perimeter of each. (b) Fencing costs Rs 60 per metre. Which plot costs more to fence, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) Both have area 300 sq m; perimeters are 70 m for A and 74 m for B. (b) B costs more: 4 x 60 = Rs 240 more.
s: Part (a): area 300 sq m each, perimeters 70 m and 74 m

questions.q: A figure of unit squares has a perimeter of 18 units. A new unit square is attached to it. (a) Find the new perimeter when it shares one side, two sides and three sides with the figure. (b) For which of these cases does the perimeter not change?
questions.a: (a) One side: 18 + 4 - 2 = 20 units; two sides: 18 + 4 - 4 = 18 units; three sides: 18 + 4 - 6 = 16 units. (b) When it shares two sides, because the two new outer sides replace the two sides that get covered.
s: Part (b): unchanged for two shared sides, with the reason

questions.q: A rectangle 12 cm by 5 cm is divided by a line parallel to its 5 cm sides into a left part of area 35 sq cm and a right part. (a) Find the area of the right part. (b) Find its dimensions.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 5 = 60 sq cm, so the right part is 60 - 35 = 25 sq cm. (b) The left part is 35 / 5 = 7 cm wide, so the right part is 12 - 7 = 5 cm wide and 5 cm tall: a 5 cm square.

questions.q: Rani says, 'With 12 unit tiles I can make rectangles whose perimeters are 26, 16 and 14 units, even though the area is the same.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Rani is right. The rectangles 1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4 all have area 12 sq units, and their perimeters are 2 x 13 = 26, 2 x 8 = 16 and 2 x 7 = 14 units. The same area can have different perimeters.
s: Lists the three rectangles with area 12

questions.q: Show that a figure made of 9 unit squares joined edge to edge cannot have a perimeter of 15 units.
questions.a: The 9 squares have 9 x 4 = 36 sides in all. Each joint hides two sides, one from each square, so the perimeter is 36 minus an even number. An even number minus an even number is even, so the perimeter is even and cannot be 15.
s: Each joint hides 2 sides, an even number
Concludes the perimeter is even, so not 15

questions.q: Make up a pair of rectangular rooms that each have an area of 36 sq m but different perimeters, and say which room needs more skirting along its walls.
questions.a: Room 1 is 6 m by 6 m with perimeter 24 m. Room 2 is 12 m by 3 m with perimeter 30 m. Both have area 36 sq m, and Room 2 needs more skirting because its perimeter is greater.
s: Two rectangles with area 36 sq m
Names the room with the greater perimeter

questions.q: A rectangular room has an area of 108 sq ft and a width of 9 ft. Find its length and its perimeter, and give the dimensions of another whole-number rectangle with a perimeter close to it but a different area.
questions.a: Length = 108 / 9 = 12 ft. Perimeter = 2 x (12 + 9) = 42 ft. A rectangle 11 ft by 10 ft has perimeter 42 ft too, with area 110 sq ft.
s: Another rectangle 11 by 10 with the same perimeter and area 110

questions.q: A shop wants a rectangular display area of 36 sq m with whole-number sides in metres. (a) List the dimensions and perimeters of all such rectangles. (b) Name the one with the least perimeter and the one with the greatest. (c) A rope costs Rs 50 per metre; find the difference in rope cost between the greatest and the least.
questions.a: (a) 1 by 36: 74 m; 2 by 18: 40 m; 3 by 12: 30 m; 4 by 9: 26 m; 6 by 6: 24 m. (b) Least: 6 m by 6 m, 24 m; greatest: 1 m by 36 m, 74 m. (c) 24 x 50 = Rs 1,200 and 74 x 50 = Rs 3,700, a difference of Rs 2,500.

questions.q: Two houses have the same floor area. House P is 36 ft by 20 ft and House Q is 30 ft by 24 ft. (a) Find the area of each. (b) Find the perimeter of each. (c) A boundary wall around the house costs Rs 700 per foot; find the wall cost for each and the difference. (d) Which house is closer to a square, and what does that tell you about its perimeter?
questions.a: (a) P: 36 x 20 = 720 sq ft; Q: 30 x 24 = 720 sq ft. (b) P: 112 ft; Q: 108 ft. (c) P: Rs 78,400; Q: Rs 75,600; difference Rs 2,800. (d) Q is closer to a square (its sides are nearer in length), and for the same area it has the smaller perimeter.
s: Part (d): Q is closer to a square with the smaller perimeter

questions.q:
A market committee has 24 identical square stalls, each 2 m by 2 m, to be placed edge to edge in one rectangular block with no gaps. A rope barrier runs around the outer edge of the block, and customers can reach only the stalls on the edge. Block X is 4 stalls by 6 stalls. Block Y is 2 stalls by 12 stalls. The rope costs Rs 15 per metre.
(a) Find the area covered by the stalls. (b) Find the perimeter of each block in metres. (c) Find the rope cost for each. (d) Y has 8 more stall fronts on the outer edge than X. Which block should the committee choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) 24 x 4 = 96 sq m for both. (b) X: 8 m by 12 m, perimeter 40 m; Y: 4 m by 24 m, perimeter 56 m. (c) X: 40 x 15 = Rs 600; Y: 56 x 15 = Rs 840. (d) Y costs Rs 240 more for 8 more stall fronts, Rs 30 per front. If the stalls earn more than that, Y pays off; if rope cost matters most, X is cheaper. Either choice is fine when it uses the figures.
s: Part (d): Rs 240 for 8 fronts and a stated choice

questions.q:
A builder offers two plots of the same area. Plot X is 36 ft by 24 ft and costs Rs 9,50,000. Plot Y is 32 ft by 27 ft and costs Rs 9,51,000. A school wants a boundary wall around the plot at Rs 900 per foot. On Plot X, a left room 12 ft wide and 24 ft deep is planned, and the remaining part is split into two rooms, the top one with an area of 240 sq ft and the full width of that remaining part.
(a) Show that the two plots have the same area. (b) Find the perimeter of each plot. (c) Find the depth of the top right room on Plot X. (d) Which plot gives the lower total cost of plot plus wall, and what would make the school pick the other?
questions.a: (a) 36 x 24 = 864 sq ft and 32 x 27 = 864 sq ft. (b) X: 2 x (36 + 24) = 120 ft; Y: 2 x (32 + 27) = 118 ft. (c) The right part is 36 - 12 = 24 ft wide, so the room's depth is 240 / 24 = 10 ft. (d) X: 9,50,000 + 120 x 900 = Rs 10,58,000. Y: 9,51,000 + 118 x 900 = Rs 10,57,200. Y is Rs 800 cheaper in total, but the gap is small, so the school might pick X if its longer side faces the road or its plan suits the rooms.
s: Part (d): totals Rs 10,58,000 and Rs 10,57,200 with a stated choice
